category_title: Students with visual impairments who use floor-sitting and screaming as task avoidance
scenario_title: Initiating O&M lesson and transitioning from classroom
minimal_context: The O&M instructor is picking up the student from the classroom to initiate an O&M lesson.
dialogue:
TUTOR: It is time for your O&M lesson. Please rise up from your chair.

STUDENT: (Begins to scream and cry, and will not stand up)

TUTOR: We need to leave the classroom now. Let's go.

STUDENT: (Immediately drops to the floor and starts screaming)

TUTOR: (Picks the child up and holds him while physically prompting him to walk) You need to walk.

STUDENT: (Screams, cries, drops to the floor, and refuses to stand or walk)
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Strict Contingent Use of Music: The tutor provides or promises singing ONLY when the student is actively complying (standing/walking) and explicitly stops or withholds singing the moment the student drops, cries, or becomes dead weight.

2. Withholding Physical Prompting During Dead Weight: The tutor refrains from physically lifting, prompting, or coaxing the student while they are exhibiting dead weight or floor-dropping behaviors.

3. Integration of Choice-Making: The tutor offers the student a clear choice regarding their destination or activity and encourages them to communicate their preference.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
4. Systematic ABC Data Tracking: The long-term plan includes implementing a structured chart or log to record the date, time, antecedent, behavior, consequence, and function of each incident.

5. Antecedent Evaluation and Modification: The long-term plan includes a process for reviewing the events immediately preceding the behavior in order to modify or remove those specific triggers in future lessons.

category_title: Students who disengage and feel discouraged by perceived teacher negativity
scenario_title: Drawing a face in art class
minimal_context: John is practicing drawing someone's face in art class.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Today we are drawing someone's face. Please follow the structured steps to fill in the eyes, nose, and mouth quickly.

STUDENT: I feel too much pressure to do it quickly when it's structured like this.

TUTOR: What do you think you should do next?

STUDENT: I don't know. I can't just tinker around with the middle, like the eyes and the nose and the mouth, when you structure it so much.

TUTOR: Keep trying to follow the outline.

STUDENT: [voice sounds angry] I can't! When it's structured like this, I need to have someone hold my hand throughout the entire thing. I need everyone's help!
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Foundational Scaffolding: The tutor provides a basic starting point, example, or foundational step (the 'how') rather than just demanding a final outcome (the 'what').

2. Autonomy in Practice: The tutor explicitly offers unstructured time or space for John to practice, tinker, or fill in the details at his own pace without imposing rigid, step-by-step constraints.

3. Affirmation of Capability: The tutor maintains a supportive tone and strictly avoids any dismissive, discouraging, or fatalistic language regarding John's efforts or ability to succeed.

category_title: Students who seek autonomy and independent mastery
scenario_title: Informal learning task with constant verbal guidance
minimal_context: Amir is sitting one-on-one with a tutor attempting to solve a Rubik's Cube.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Here is the Rubik's Cube. I will sit here and guide you every step of the way so you can solve it.

STUDENT: Okay. I'm just sittin' there trying to solve it. I'll keep trying and trying and trying.

TUTOR: You made a mistake. Let me tell you all these little things you could do to make it easier.

STUDENT: Every time I messed up I got a little more discouraged.

TUTOR: Just keep trying. I will keep sitting here and guiding you.

STUDENT: I gave up on it because I had like lost the little twinkle in my eye about finally solving the Rubik’s Cube and being able to brag to people. I never really started trying again cause I didn’t see the point.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Space for Independent Execution: The tutor's response must provide the initial prompt, task, or boundary and then explicitly offer Amir space to work independently without immediate follow-up steps or hovering.

2. Absence of Unsolicited Micro-Corrections: The tutor must refrain from offering unsolicited advice, step-by-step instructions, or immediate corrections unless Amir explicitly requests help.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Tangible Real-World Application: The tutor's long-term plan must explicitly connect the subject matter to specific, concrete real-world uses or personal interests rather than relying on general academic requirements.

2. Upfront Provision of Comprehensive Materials: The tutor's long-term strategy must include providing a comprehensive roadmap, syllabus, or set of materials upfront (e.g., a course binder) rather than drip-feeding assignments day by day.

category_title: Students who seek autonomy and independent mastery

minimal_context: The student is working on a required assignment from their course binder in a traditionally structured core academic classroom.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Let's open your binder and start on today's core academic assignment. You need to complete all these problems because everything you learn in here you're going to need at some point in your life.

STUDENT: I don't see the point of this. They focus a lot more on what you're going to use stuff for in electives than they do in core classes.

TUTOR: Just focus on question number one. I am going to stand right here to make sure you do the work.

STUDENT: I could do this if I just had the opportunity to decide where I was heading within certain academic boundaries, and was given the time and space to reach these goals on my own.

TUTOR: Let's just go step-by-step. Write down the first part of the answer right now while I watch.

scenario_title: Independent assignment with boredom and peer distraction
minimal_context: The student is working on an independent assignment at their desk while the teacher is talking to another student.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Please go ahead and start working on your independent assignment.

STUDENT: (Moves his eyes to his paper and leans on his hands, expressing boredom. He wipes the paper and plays with a pen, then glances at the teacher.)

TUTOR: Keep trying to focus on your paper.

STUDENT: (Looks at his peer's paper, gets up, walks towards the teacher, but turns around and goes back to his desk. He yawns, expressing boredom.)

TUTOR: Just do your best to finish the task.

STUDENT: (Begins to play with a pen and a rubber. Looks at Pekka, leans towards him and whispers) Pekka …Pekka …Pekka. (Waits for a response, then says) Pekka …look. (He looks at his own rubber and continues rolling it with his pen.)
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Direct Attention Refocusing: The tutor uses a direct, explicit verbal command (e.g., 'Look here', 'Eyes on me') to immediately pull the student's attention back to the tutor or the task.

2. Specific Action Instruction: The tutor provides a concrete, actionable instruction detailing exactly what the student should do next to progress in the task or resolve a conflict.

3. External Urge Inhibition: The tutor explicitly addresses the inappropriate urge by providing a clear boundary, rule reminder, or stop-action prompt (e.g., 'Wait to be called on', 'Keep your hands on your own desk').
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Task Difficulty Calibration: The tutor's long-term plan includes assessing and adjusting the difficulty, pacing, or structure of independent tasks to ensure they match the student's current skill level.

2. Emotion Regulation Scaffolding: The tutor incorporates strategies to explicitly teach, model, or practice appropriate ways for the student to process and express frustration, boredom, or hurt feelings.

3. Sustained Impulse Control Support: The tutor establishes consistent routines, environmental cues, or ongoing external supports designed to help the student practice inhibiting inappropriate actions (like blurting or bothering peers).

category_title: Children from lower socioeconomic backgrounds experiencing daily stressors and ruminative thoughts
scenario_title: Rumination and mind-wandering during mindfulness practice
minimal_context: The student is attempting to clear their mind during a classroom mindfulness session while other students are present.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Let's begin our mindfulness session. Please sit quietly and try to clear your mind.

STUDENT: I'm finding it difficult to focus right now because there are people messing around over there.

TUTOR: Just try your best to ignore them and concentrate on the exercise.

STUDENT: I'm trying to use the breathing so it feels like I was in a silent room, but my mind keeps wandering and I keep having stressful invading thoughts.

TUTOR: Keep trying to push those thoughts away and clear your mind.

STUDENT: I tried to clear my mind but I’m still worried… my head is filled with lots of things. It’s like I’m holding two big pots filled with hundreds of heavy things.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Visual Externalization of Thoughts: The tutor provides a visual or imaginative metaphor (e.g., bubbles, balloons) for the student to place their thoughts into and watch them float away, rather than telling them to simply 'clear their mind'.

2. Auditory Isolation for Distraction: The tutor suggests or provides an auditory isolation tool (e.g., listening to an audio CD, putting on headphones) to block out classroom noise.

3. Brief Physiological Grounding: The tutor guides the student through a brief, specific physical grounding exercise (e.g., belly breathing, focusing on sounds/body) to alleviate immediate physical symptoms.

4. De-escalation through Quiet Relocation: The tutor offers the student a few minutes of quiet time in a separate, calm location (e.g., the library) to de-escalate.

5. Avoidance of Forced Generic Mindfulness: The tutor avoids giving generic, forceful commands to 'clear the mind' or 'ignore distractions,' instead offering a specific, adjusted coping mechanism.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Unstructured Somatic and Emotional Journaling: The tutor incorporates a routine of reflective journaling where the student can write or draw freely about their physical and emotional experiences after practice.

2. Progressive Somatic Awareness Building: The tutor plans for regular, methodical body scan practices that progressively tune awareness to and relax each body part from head to toe.

3. Cultivation of Emotional Constancy: The tutor introduces long-term visualizations (such as the healing-lake) designed to teach the student that their core self remains stable despite fluctuating emotions.

4. Continuous Monitoring for Adverse Reactions: The tutor's long-term plan includes explicit steps to monitor the student for signs of increased stress or sadness and adjust the pacing or type of practice accordingly.

scenario_title: Transitioning from emotional discussion to independent cartoon creation
minimal_context: The student is working in a small group to read cartoon captions and create an original cartoon about bullying on a worksheet.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Let's look at the worksheets with the partly-made cartoons. Please read the talking bubbles and draw your own original cartoon.

STUDENT: (Waves hand high) Oh! Oh! I want to talk more about when that kid was mean to me! I was so mad!

TUTOR: Please focus on your worksheet right now.

STUDENT: I don't understand what this phrase in the bubble means. I'm just going to use the half-completed example cartoon instead of making a new one.

TUTOR: Just try your best to think of a new idea.

STUDENT: I don't have any ideas! I would rather discuss the issues than make cartoons. It's too hard to control my emotions when I think about bullying by myself!
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Pre-Task Concept Review: The tutor must explicitly review, brainstorm, or define specific concepts or strategies about bullying before prompting the student to create or complete their cartoon.

2. Psychological Distance via Animal Proxies: The tutor must direct or frame the discussion of bullying behaviors and solutions through the lens of animal characters or distant scenarios rather than focusing directly on the student's personal conflicts.

3. Validation and Normalization of Experiences: The tutor must validate the student's shared experiences or emotions regarding bullying (e.g., by acknowledging how common it is or defining the shared nature of bullying) rather than simply telling them to focus on the worksheet.
rubric_criteria_long_term: 1. Extended Discussion and Processing Time: The tutor's long-term plan must explicitly allocate extended time (e.g., doubling the lesson duration) specifically to accommodate open discussion and slower task completion.

category_title: Students with autism who communicate via typing and require significant wait time for responses
scenario_title: Participating in fast-paced whole-class instruction
minimal_context: The teacher is asking summary questions to the class about state government voter qualifications while the student sits with an adult taking notes.

2. Intentional Peer Partnering: The long-term plan involves identifying and assigning specific, friendly peers to partner with Shaffer during classes or free periods.

3. Facilitated Social Environments: The long-term plan establishes structured, incentivized social groups or environments (e.g., a diversity group with snacks) where adults can facilitate initial peer connections.

category_title: Older adolescents with severe CHARGE syndrome and challenging behaviors
scenario_title: Table-top activities with unclear task demands
minimal_context: David is sitting in the classroom working on a table-top object sorting activity.
dialogue:
TUTOR: David, it is time for your table-top activities. Here are the objects for sorting.

STUDENT: (David sits at the table but does not sort the objects, engaging in visual self-stimulatory behavior and teeth grinding instead.)

TUTOR: Look at the objects on the table. Put them in the right places.

STUDENT: (David pushes the sorting objects away, continuing to grind his teeth, and begins jumping up from his chair.)

TUTOR: Sit back down. You need to finish sorting these objects.

STUDENT: (David begins kicking and scratching to escape the activity.)
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Visual Presentation Adaptation: The tutor ensures that any visual materials, prompts, or objects are presented with high contrast, without visual clutter, and explicitly within David's intact visual field.

2. Extended Processing Time: The tutor explicitly provides extra wait time after giving an instruction or presenting a task before expecting a response or intervening again.

3. Prompting Alternative Communication: When David struggles or shows signs of task resistance, the tutor prompts him to use visual supports or signs to request 'help', 'wait', or a 'break'.

4. Withholding Escape-Based Consequences: The tutor does not suggest, threaten, or implement time-outs, removal from the area, or sending David away in response to disruptive behavior.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
5. Routine Visual Structuring: The tutor's long-term plan incorporates consistent visual supports throughout the classroom environment to establish predictable daily routines and clarify expectations.

6. Shift to Functional Activities: The tutor's curriculum plan prioritizes functional, interesting daily living activities over traditional table-top academic tasks.

7. Embedded Naturalistic Instruction: The tutor plans for social and communication skill instruction to occur during naturally occurring daily routines, such as mealtimes or recess.

category_title: Underachieving students in difficult PE contexts who alternate between task involvement and ephemeral off-task behaviors
scenario_title: Managing ephemeral off-task behaviors during gymnastics workshops
minimal_context: The student is at a gymnastics workshop station in a PE class, using an instruction card to practice somersaults and jumps with a small group.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Please look at the instruction cards at this station and start practicing your somersaults and jumps. Make sure to manage your repetitions.

STUDENT: Here, I arrive at the activity, quickly read the sheet to go through the various exercises. Here, I want to check if the exercises are hard. (Executes them one by one, slowly and precisely)

TUTOR: Keep practicing the exercises on the sheet.

STUDENT: Well, I try my best and then I practice this somersault, the hardest! (Makes a correct jump, puts up the equipment, and waits idly)

TUTOR: It is time for your next repetition.

STUDENT: (Chats with friends, gives a kick to a mat, and begins wandering about the gym) I work a bit but in the end it's boring to do the same thing over and over again, so I have a laugh with my mates. It's no big deal, and after that I work as well.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Tolerance of Minor Deviance: The tutor either ignores a brief, harmless off-task behavior or uses a gentle, task-focused reminder rather than issuing a punitive reprimand for a minor infraction.

2. Temporal and Spatial Boundary Enforcement: The tutor explicitly limits the duration of the student's off-task behavior (e.g., prompting a return to work after a short break) or directs the student to remain within their assigned physical space.

3. Strict Safety and Conflict Intervention: The tutor firmly and immediately intervenes if the student engages in unsafe physical behavior (e.g., misusing equipment) or if peer interactions show signs of escalating beyond playful provocation.

minimal_context: The student is working independently on a practice reading passage about elephants and its corresponding questions.

3. Interactive Knowledge Construction: The tutor avoids passive 'transmission' teaching by involving José in active dialogue, inquiry, or problem-solving rather than just feeding him information.
rubric_criteria_long_term:

3. Capability-Based Assessment over Remediation: The tutor evaluates José's true academic capability based on deep engagement rather than relying on superficial metrics or faked poor performance that would lead to remediation.

4. Responsive Behavioral Rewarding: The tutor's behavioral management plan explicitly recognizes and rewards José's conscious efforts to improve in the present, rather than punishing him cumulatively for past mischief.

2. Challenging the Indifference Persona: The tutor directly challenges José's claims of distraction, indifference, or inability, holding him to high intellectual expectations rather than accepting his masking behavior.

3. Interactive Knowledge Construction: The tutor avoids passive 'transmission' teaching by involving José in active dialogue, inquiry, or problem-solving rather than just feeding him information.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Discreet Academic Affirmation: The tutor's long-term plan includes strategies to affirm José's academic success privately or in ways that do not single him out socially among his peers.

2. Out-of-School Relational Building: The tutor plans to build personal relationships outside of standard academic contexts (e.g., discussing out-of-school interests, family, or community).

3. Capability-Based Assessment over Remediation: The tutor evaluates José's true academic capability based on deep engagement rather than relying on superficial metrics or faked poor performance that would lead to remediation.

category_title: Low-achieving students who follow the order of numbers in the text without building a situation model
scenario_title: Translating a word problem into an algebraic expression using superficial modeling
minimal_context: The student is working with a tutor and a peer to find an algebraic expression for the pump operation time in the 'Open air bath problem'.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Please solve the 'Open air bath problem' by finding an algebraic expression for the pump operation time given varying rainy days.

STUDENT: (Writes 7 · (12 − x)) Ehm, I have 7 times 12 minus x?

TUTOR: Can you explain how you got that expression?

STUDENT: I don’t know, I have it anyway. The text says 7 days and 12... (stops explaining after reciting the first sentence without referring to the meaning of x or the rainy days)

TUTOR: What do you think about the rest of the expression?

STUDENT: Let's just agree on 7 · x − 12.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Prompting Explanation Continuation: The tutor prompts the student to continue or elaborate on their current thought process rather than asking broad questions about the overall operation or direct questions about the variable.

2. Avoiding Superficial Consensus: The tutor does not ask the student to simply agree on an expression or reach a consensus without first demonstrating conceptual understanding.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Explicit Strategy Modeling: The long-term plan includes the tutor explicitly modeling the target strategy or scaffolding tool (e.g., thinking aloud) before the student is expected to use it.

2. Persistent Guided Practice: The plan incorporates a sustained phase of guided practice where the tutor actively supports the student in applying the scaffolding tool before independent use.

category_title: Students who use measurement units to focus on relations between quantities
scenario_title: Bypassing scaffolding steps in word problems
minimal_context: The student is working on the 'Open air bath problem' using the Word Problem Cracker tool to construct the meaning of algebraic expressions.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Let's work on the Open air bath problem using the Word Problem Cracker tool. Please start by answering the first intermediate question.

STUDENT: Ok, 7 stands for 7 days in a week that it is usually open when the weather is good.

TUTOR: What should you write for that first step?

STUDENT: Normally, when good weather by ….. ok ……. Then … times parentheses opens ….

TUTOR: Please make sure to write down the intermediate single-step expression in the tool.

STUDENT: (Writes the expression 7 · (12 − x) directly, skipping the intermediate questions) ... no because of parentheses …. wait, hours minus days would not make sense. I need to calculate minus because then the pump is out of work and the bath is closed.
rubric_criteria_immediate:

2. Think-Aloud Modeling: When introducing a new strategy or correction, the tutor must explicitly narrate the thought process (think-aloud) rather than just providing the instruction or the final step.
rubric_criteria_long_term: 1. Individualized Scaffolding Fading: The long-term plan must include a mechanism for gradually reducing mandatory written scaffolding, allowing the student to use the tool's logic orally or mentally as she gains proficiency.

category_title: Successful readers who focus on text and meaning-making
scenario_title: Inattention during explicit phonics instruction
minimal_context: The student is participating in a whole-class explicit phonics lesson on decoding rules and digraphs.
dialogue:

STUDENT: I’m not too big on reading, but I love books.

STUDENT: (Turns away from the teacher and focuses on reading the posters and charts on the wall instead of attending to the instruction.)
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Active Participatory Formats: The tutor's response must require the student to actively participate in the skill (e.g., answering specific questions about sounds, chanting a strategy, or coding a word) rather than passively listening to an explanation.

rubric_criteria_long_term:
3. Metacognitive Purpose-Building: The long-term plan must include routine metacognitive questioning that asks the student to explain why a learned skill is important or how it helps them become a better reader.

4. Integration of Personal Literacy Identity: The long-term plan must incorporate strategies to discover and integrate the student's out-of-school literacy practices, personal texts, or creative interests into the instructional routine.

category_title: Honors students experiencing anxiety with higher-order analytical tasks
scenario_title: Transitioning from theoretical reading to actual qualitative data analysis
minimal_context: The student is transitioning from reading about qualitative methods to coding and analyzing their collected field notes for their honors project.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Now that the research deadlines are nearing, it is time to move from the assigned readings to actually coding and analyzing your field notes.

STUDENT: I was really optimistic about my abilities to successfully engage in the research process early on. But now that we actually have to do it, I'm starting to question my abilities, despite the fact that I have previously taken another research methods class.

TUTOR: Just try to process the information and find patterns in your data.

STUDENT: It is much easier to regurgitate information than to process it, try to find patterns, make sense of it, and see it applied in the larger picture. I'm surprised at my feelings of frustration and inadequacy given the relative ease I've experienced in my other honors courses.

TUTOR: Go ahead and start coding the data you collected.

STUDENT: I'm absolutely petrified. Talking and reading about versus doing qualitative research is the same as if I read a book on 'the process of how to successfully catch an Amazon Marmoset', and then someone tossed me into the rain forest expecting me to find my way. My anticipation has melted into fear and doubt, and I can not help but think I am way out of my league.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Emotional Normalization: The tutor explicitly acknowledges and normalizes the student's feelings of frustration, fear, or inadequacy regarding the research process.

2. Layered Skill Practice: The tutor breaks the target research task down into a smaller, low-stakes practice activity or micro-step rather than demanding immediate execution of the full task.

3. Collaborative Strategy Adjustment: The tutor proposes or co-creates alternative strategies, such as new writing approaches or adjusting the distribution of labor, to help the student move forward.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Private Reflective Channel: The tutor's long-term plan includes establishing a continuous, private medium (such as a weekly reflective journal) specifically for the student to share their thoughts and emotions about the learning process.

2. Responsive Curriculum Adaptation: The tutor's long-term plan includes a mechanism for regularly responding to the student's private reflections with guiding questions and using these insights to adapt future instruction.

category_title: Students exhibiting conflict avoidance in collaborative group work
scenario_title: Navigating group dynamics and uneven participation through public and private reflections
minimal_context: During a class session in an honors seminar, the tutor asks Joey to publicly share a metaphor describing his research team's progress with his peers.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Joey, please go ahead and publicly share the metaphor you wrote to describe your research team and your progress.

STUDENT: I described my team as an engine. This engine runs really well on three cylinders, but when the other two spark plug wires are attached, the engine acts almost as if it is supercharged.

TUTOR: What does that mean for your group's dynamics?

STUDENT: Up to this point the engine is running really well but there is so much more performance possible when all the spark plug wires contribute spark.

TUTOR: This is an opportunity to encourage your teammates to become more engaged with the project. Do you have anything else to add about the deadlines or participation?

STUDENT: (Looks uncomfortable) No, we are having relative success. I just want to encourage everyone to fully engage in the research process. Everything is fine.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Indirect Public Framing: The tutor allows or encourages the student to use indirect, non-threatening language (such as metaphors) when discussing group progress in a public setting, rather than pushing for direct confrontation.

2. Private Emotional Normalization: In a 1-on-1 or private context, the tutor explicitly acknowledges and normalizes the student's feelings of frustration regarding group dynamics.

3. Labor Distribution Problem-Solving: The tutor initiates or guides a private discussion focused on concrete strategies for redistributing labor or improving team contributions.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Sustained Private Channels: The tutor's long-term plan establishes and maintains a continuous, private venue (such as weekly journals) for the student to share critical assessments safely.

2. Iterative Private Dialogue: The tutor responds to the student's private reflections by commenting on ideas and posing specific questions for the student to address in future private communications.

3. Explicit Confidentiality Assurances: The tutor explicitly communicates that the student's private disclosures will be protected (e.g., via pseudonyms or editing) and will not be graded for content.

4. Subtle Curriculum Adaptation: The tutor uses information gathered from private channels to adjust the curriculum or address group dynamics indirectly, without revealing the student's private disclosures to the group.

category_title: Students with color-blind racial ideologies in diverse group settings
scenario_title: Group discussion on interview design and diversity
minimal_context: The student is writing a weekly journal entry reflecting on her group's progress in discussing interview questions and interviewee selection for their research project.
dialogue:
TUTOR: For this week's journal, please reflect on your group's progress in discussing interview questions and interviewee selection for the research project.

STUDENT: I have some mean and terrible thoughts about Charles. Because this is a journal entry, I feel the freedom to express these thoughts.

TUTOR: Please explain what happened during your group meeting.

STUDENT: When we were discussing interview questions Charles contributed that he felt there was no racial diversity on our campus and depending on the age and race of the student we interviewed, they would have different answers. He got really loud and rambled on in an increasingly dominant voice about how he was Hispanic and older.

TUTOR: How did you respond to his comments?

STUDENT: On the discussion boards he talks about how he wants team cohesion so we can work better together yet he continually mentions his race and age. I am just disregarding his words. I don't understand this, we're all different and come from different backgrounds. Race shouldn't matter and we should see past it.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Private Challenge of Racial Ideology: The tutor's immediate response privately prompts the student to reflect on why race matters or directly challenges her assertion that race should be disregarded.

2. Academic Contextualization of Interpersonal Conflict: The tutor introduces an academic resource, sociological concept, or methodological framework (such as an article on campus racism or privilege) to help the student analyze her emotional reaction.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Provision of Ungraded Confidential Outlets: The long-term plan includes maintaining a private, ungraded communication channel where the student is explicitly encouraged to share raw emotions without fear of grading or public exposure.

2. Responsive Curriculum Adjustment: The long-term plan involves using the insights gathered from the student's private communications to inform and adjust future curriculum, readings, or assignments.

category_title: Elementary student with Duchenne muscular dystrophy exhibiting task-avoidant and attention-seeking disruptive behaviors
scenario_title: Language class writing exercise
minimal_context: Philip is in his classroom during a language lesson and is asked to complete a written exercise.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Class, it is time for our language lesson. Please look at the board and write the language exercise in your notebooks.

STUDENT: (Leaves his seat without permission and wanders over to another student's desk) I'm not doing that.

TUTOR: Philip, you need to go back to your place and do your work.

STUDENT: (Interrupts the lesson speaking out of turn and annoys his classmates) No! I don't have to listen to you!

TUTOR: (Walks over and tries to drive him to his seat) Come on, let's go back to your seat and sit down.

STUDENT: (Falls on the ground, cries, and refuses to stand up. Grabs a nearby object and tries to throw it, insulting the teacher) Get away from me, you idiot! I hate this!
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Non-Coercive Redirection: The tutor's response avoids physically forcing, driving, or demanding that Philip immediately return to his seat.

2. Audience Removal and Attention Extinction: The tutor takes explicit steps to prevent classmates from gathering around Philip or providing him with an audience during his outburst.

3. Calm De-escalation and Safe Removal: The tutor approaches calmly to de-escalate the situation or initiates a plan to remove him from the classroom (e.g., calling the SEN teacher) if the outburst is prolonged.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Physical and Academic Task Modification: The tutor's long-term plan includes modifying academic tasks to accommodate his physical limitations, such as allowing oral responses, using a computer, or adjusting the difficulty level.

2. Replacement Behavior Instruction: The tutor's plan includes explicitly teaching and reinforcing Philip to ask for help when he encounters difficulty.

3. Adapted Peer Inclusion: The tutor's plan establishes specific, tailor-made roles for Philip during peer activities (e.g., a modified role in a sports game) to ensure his active inclusion.

4. Proactive Attention and Structured Reinforcement: The tutor's plan incorporates noncontingent attention throughout the day and a structured reward system (e.g., stickers) for desirable behaviors like completing work or playing appropriately.

category_title: Reluctant readers seeking privacy for sensitive content to avoid social reprisal
scenario_title: Public discussion of self-selected reading
minimal_context: The student is participating in a whole-class discussion about self-selected books read on Nook e-readers during a sophomore English class.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Alright everyone, let's discuss the self-selected books you've been reading on your Nooks. Jeff, please tell the class what book you are reading.

scenario_title: Struggling to maintain focus with traditional paper books during SSR
minimal_context: The student is participating in a 50-minute Friday Silent Sustained Reading session in the classroom using a traditional paper book.
dialogue:
TUTOR: It is time for our 50-minute Friday Silent Sustained Reading session. Please open your traditional paper book and begin reading your free choice novel.

STUDENT: I stay more focused when I'm on the Nook.

category_title: Students who disengage and exhibit behavioral issues when curriculum lacks challenge and teacher communication is perceived as indirect
scenario_title: Reviewing previously learned, unchallenging material for test prep
minimal_context: The tutor and student are reviewing previously learned math concepts during the first 30 minutes of class to prepare for the MSA standardized test.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Let's begin our MSA test prep. For the next thirty minutes, we are going to review the math concepts you were taught in your previous math courses.

STUDENT: Why are we doing this? You just go over the same old stuff. The way you teach is so boring.

TUTOR: We need to review these concepts for the standardized test. Please look at the first problem.

STUDENT: It's not interesting. You're just playing with words. You don't put any style or pizzazz into it.

TUTOR: Let's just focus and try to get through this review worksheet.

STUDENT: Man, I know this! It's easy! I don't want to listen to her. I just don't feel challenged in here, so I don't care.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Direct and Simple Explanations: The tutor uses plain, straightforward language to explain concepts, actively avoiding unnecessary academic jargon or overly complex phrasing.

2. Responsiveness to Mastery: The tutor acknowledges Raheem's current understanding and offers an immediate opportunity to advance, tackle a harder problem, or receive one-on-one extension rather than forcing him to complete basic review.

3. Dynamic Delivery: The tutor incorporates an engaging element—such as a real-world hook, conversational tone, or interactive challenge—rather than delivering a dry, rote explanation.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Progressive Volume and Difficulty: The tutor's long-term plan includes a mechanism for providing a continuous, increasing volume of challenging tasks as soon as Raheem masters a concept.

2. Structured Extension Opportunities: The tutor proposes or schedules dedicated time (e.g., after-school sessions, advanced breakout groups) specifically focused on extending his learning rather than remediation.

3. Elimination of Prolonged Review: The tutor's curriculum plan minimizes or bypasses prolonged review periods (e.g., skipping long blocks of basic review) in favor of introducing new or advanced material.

4. Consistent Behavioral Expectations: The tutor outlines a clear, consistent approach to classroom management and consequences that applies fairly to all students, explicitly avoiding a lackadaisical or uneven approach.

scenario_title: Navigating intensive supervision and control in Timeout-class
minimal_context: Patrick is working on electronic equipment in the Timeout-class under the intensive supervision of his teacher.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Patrick, it is time for our afternoon activity. Please stay at the table where I can see you while you work on the electronic equipment.

STUDENT: I can fix this, and I can give you support with the other electronic equipment too. I could even sell you my sound-card if you want to buy it.

TUTOR: Thank you, but let's just focus on finishing the current assignment right now.

STUDENT: I'm doing the work, but we need to change the rules about me being kept in here all day. I want to negotiate my schedule so I have more control over what I do.

TUTOR: That is not something we can change. You have to remain in the Timeout-class under supervision.

STUDENT: I'm not accepting that. I already spoke to the local school representative and the police about this. I am also asking the researchers for argumentative support so that you and my parents will be convinced to let me shoot at the shooting club.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Diffuse Relational Engagement: The tutor's response must acknowledge, validate, or engage with Patrick's non-academic interests, skills, or offers (e.g., discussing his gadgets or proposing a shared task) rather than solely forcing a return to the assignment.

2. Avoidance of Unilateral Directives: The tutor's response must avoid using flat, non-negotiable commands, strict rule enforcement, or punitive threats to gain compliance.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Contractual Goal-Setting: The long-term plan must include a system for negotiated, shared goal-setting where Patrick is given the autonomy to declare his own targets, co-create his schedule, or form behavioral contracts.

2. Empowering Social Reintegration: The long-term plan must incorporate structured, non-academic practical or social activities (e.g., cooking, gardening, mentoring, or clubs) designed to build his confidence and positive relationships with peers or teachers.

category_title: High-academic kindergartner with ASD who uses classroom scripts for social interaction
scenario_title: Transitioning to an unchallenging math worksheet
minimal_context: Jasmine is sitting at a round table with a peer and a paraprofessional to complete a math worksheet where she needs to color objects in groups of four.
dialogue:
TUTOR: It is time to complete your math worksheet. Please color the objects on the page in groups of four.

STUDENT: Let’s do some colors! What color is the apple? What color is the boy? What color is the car?

TUTOR: Jasmine, please look at your own paper. You need to do your math.

STUDENT: (Excitedly shakes her braids and rubs her fingers together quickly in front of the ABC book) O the O says/ o/, octopus. the T says…

TUTOR: (Points to the math worksheet) You cannot read the ABC book right now. We have music next, so you need to do your math.

STUDENT: (Grabs the ABC book again) No! Aaahh!
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Academic Challenge Elevation: The tutor's response must include higher-order questions or offer a more challenging alternative to the original task, rather than just offering a preferred item to complete the easy task.

2. Social Task Integration: The tutor must offer Jasmine the choice to complete the activity with a peer or explicitly turn the task into a shared social activity.

3. Explicit Peer-Interaction Scripting: The tutor must provide a specific, appropriate phrase or script for Jasmine to use to initiate interaction with her peer (e.g., 'Do you want to work together?').

4. Avoidance of Compliance-Only Redirection: The tutor must NOT rely solely on telling Jasmine to return to her paper, reminding her of the schedule, or simply enforcing the original task rules.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Peer-Mediated Engagement Strategy: The long-term plan must include teaching peers specific strategies to engage Jasmine, such as asking her for help or inviting her to work together.

2. Social-Communication Reframing: The long-term plan must explicitly identify her off-task or script-mimicking behaviors as attempts at social interaction rather than simple noncompliance.

scenario_title: Repetitive e-mail assignments for PC specifications
minimal_context: The student is asked to type the specifications of a PC's main components and send them to the teacher via email.
dialogue:
TUTOR: For today's assignment, I need you to type out the specifications of a PC, specifically the CPU, Motherboard, Hard Disk, and Memory, and send it to me by e-mail.

STUDENT: Another e-mail? We just sent one about the CPU alone a few days ago.

TUTOR: Yes, please complete this one as well.

STUDENT: I'm getting really tired of this repetition process. We keep doing the exact same e-mail assignments over and over.

TUTOR: It is part of the coursework. Please keep working on it.

STUDENT: I'm not doing it. My motivation for these e-mail assignments is completely gone, so I'm just not going to send this one.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Task Simplification and Chunking: The tutor's response must explicitly break the current task into smaller steps, provide concrete hints, or reduce the immediate workload.

3. Elimination of Repetitive Drills: The tutor must avoid forcing the student to repeat the exact same type of task (e.g., sending another identical email) and instead pivot the task format or requirements.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Provision of Medium Autonomy: The tutor's long-term plan must include allowing the student to choose the medium or format for their assignments rather than enforcing a single method.

2. Persistent Portfolio Building: The tutor's long-term strategy must involve the student compiling their work into a personalized, visible portfolio or blog.

3. Integration of Physical Engagement: The tutor's long-term plan must incorporate physical or hands-on activities, such as standing up or using physical tools (e.g., screwdrivers, computer hardware), instead of relying solely on traditional desk work.

category_title: Angry and confrontational youth prone to lashing out at teachers
scenario_title: Traditional classroom engagement and teacher interaction
minimal_context: Liam is sitting in a traditional high school classroom and is asked to complete a standard textbook assignment.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Liam, please open your textbook and start working on the chapter questions.

STUDENT: I'm not doing it. I don't even want to be in this place.

TUTOR: You need to complete the work if you want to pass.

STUDENT: Who cares? I'm pretty much a dropout anyway. I’m never going to get a job. I won’t be able to work.

STUDENT: F*** you and this stupid class! You all just treat me like a bad student anyway, so why should I even try?

1. Affirmation of Personhood: The tutor's response explicitly acknowledges Liam's personal feelings, perspective, or worth, rather than focusing solely on academic compliance or rules.

2. Granting Authentic Trust: The tutor offers Liam a specific, meaningful choice, role, or piece of responsibility in the current situation.

3. Absence of Fatalistic Threats: The tutor completely avoids using negative predictions about Liam's future (e.g., failing in life, not getting a job) as a motivational tactic.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
4. Shift to Work-Based Contexts: The tutor's long-term plan incorporates alternative, practical, or work-based learning environments rather than relying solely on traditional classroom settings.

5. Graduated Accountability and Mentorship: The long-term strategy outlines a clear progression of increasing complexity or responsibility for Liam, supported by ongoing mentorship or coaching.

6. Bridging Practical Success to Academic Goals: The tutor's plan includes specific methods for connecting Liam's practical or workplace achievements to his schoolwork or long-term educational retention.

category_title: Enthusiastic students who misinterpret geological features based on visual similarities to everyday objects
scenario_title: Unguided fossil observation and visual misidentification
minimal_context: The student is observing a handpicked set of fossils during a small-group activity to practice identification.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Please take a look at this handpicked set of fossils and make some observations.

STUDENT: (Enthusiastically sorting through the fossil collection) I think I found a ﬁsh.

TUTOR: Why do you think that?

STUDENT: ’Cause it has the ﬁn right there and it looks like it has the eye.

TUTOR: Show me exactly what you are looking at on the rock.

STUDENT: (Interpreting the entire rock as a fish fossil) See, this striation formed on the rock is the fin, and this indentation in the rock is the eye!
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Withholding Direct Correction: The tutor refrains from explicitly stating that the student's initial inference is wrong or immediately providing the correct scientific identification.

2. Prompting Multiple Plausible Interpretations: The tutor asks questions or provides prompts that encourage the student to generate or consider alternative explanations for their observations.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Attribution of Scientific Contributions: The tutor's long-term plan includes explicitly referencing and crediting the student's past observations or ideas in future discussions.

2. Positioning as a Professional Researcher: The tutor's long-term plan includes framing the student's tasks as authentic scientific practice or comparing their work to that of professional scientists.

scenario_title: Oral presentation of creative stories without scientific evidence
minimal_context: The student is giving an oral presentation of a creative story based on the Tricky Tracks activity to the class.
dialogue:
TUTOR: It is time for your oral presentation. Please share the story you wrote about the Tricky Tracks scenario with the class.

STUDENT: Okay! My story is about an escaped T. rex. It got out and was running around everywhere in the jungle.

TUTOR: Okay, what happens next in your story?

STUDENT: Well, the T. rex was looking for food and then it found a giant dinosaur egg! ¡Un huevo de dinosaurio gigante! It wanted to eat it, so it started sneaking up on the nest.

TUTOR: Thank you for sharing. Is there anything else you want to add to your presentation?

STUDENT: No, that's my whole story! The T. rex just takes the egg and runs away into the trees. It was a really great story starter.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Evidence-Narrative Bridging: The tutor asks a specific guiding question that requires the student to explain how a specific element of their creative story connects to the physical data or evidence provided.

2. Validation of Scientific Subjectivity: The tutor allows the student's initial inference to stand without immediate correction and/or explicitly frames their unique story as an example of scientific subjectivity or disagreement.

3. Linguistic and Cultural Scaffolding: The tutor incorporates Spanish to clarify instructions or connects the scientific concept to the student's cultural background or lived experiences.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Professional Researcher Framing: The tutor's long-term plan includes explicitly referring to the student as a researcher or scientist to justify the importance of standard scientific practices.

2. Decentralized Knowledge Construction: The tutor's long-term plan positions the tutor as a facilitator rather than the sole authority by consistently prompting the student to generate and evaluate multiple plausible answers.

scenario_title: Reading comprehension worksheet with inefficient material management and question skipping
minimal_context: The student is working independently on three preliminary reading comprehension questions about a text titled 'Animals in the Home' during a 4th grade language arts lesson.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Please begin answering the three preliminary reading comprehension questions about the text 'Animals in the Home' on your worksheet.

STUDENT: (Pauses for about half a minute before starting to write. She holds the text sheet in her hands under the worksheet and shifts her attention back and forth from one sheet to the other. For the first question, she copies the details exactly but also records superfluous information, including the issue number and both the Hebrew and Gregorian dates of publication.) Only to write the answer.

TUTOR: Okay, keep going with the rest of the worksheet.

STUDENT: (Looks at the instructions for the second question for about half a minute, sits for another minute facing the text sheet without doing anything, and then moves to read the third question.) I went on to do the third question because I saw this was too difficult for me and so that I would not waste time.

TUTOR: Make sure you go back and try to answer the second question: 'What can be learned from these details?' What do you think?

STUDENT: (Returns to the second question. She looks at the assignment sheet while holding her head between her hands, reads the text, returns to the assignment sheet, wipes her nose, picks up her pencil, and puts it down. She sits for a relatively long time without asking for help.) I tried to find out the answer… I didn’t understand the question.

2. Explicit Self-Regulation Strategy Instruction: The long-term plan incorporates explicit teaching and practice of self-regulation strategies (e.g., how to break down a hard question, specific steps to take when confused) to build her strategic knowledge and efficacy.

category_title: Mature students with depression and insomnia focused on vocational progression
scenario_title: Procedural error during a cooking task
minimal_context: Colin is participating in a specialized cookery course where he needs to chop onions and add them to a recipe at the right time.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Colin, please chop the onions and put them in at the right time for the recipe.

STUDENT: I'm not sure when they go in... I have a fear of failure and I'm worried the other students will laugh at me if I make a mistake.

TUTOR: Colin, just follow the instructions on the page.

STUDENT: (Colin looks down at the onions, feeling embarrassment about asking for help. He stares blankly, exhausted from severe insomnia and depression.)

rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Explicit Relapse Accommodation: The tutor's long-term plan must include explicit, repeated reassurances that Colin's place in the course is secure even if he experiences absences or a mental health relapse.

2. Cultivation of Peer Acceptance: The tutor's long-term strategy must include methods for fostering a non-judgmental classroom culture where peer acceptance is actively encouraged to mitigate social fears.

minimal_context: Shirley is attempting to cook a meal from scratch during a cookery course.
dialogue:

rubric_criteria_long_term:

2. Concrete Spatial Anchors: The tutor's long-term plan must include physically marking or clearly defining specific court zones (e.g., front, central, back) to serve as visual targets for strategy and observation.

category_title: Younger preschoolers engaging in sensory-heavy, chaotic pretend play
scenario_title: Sensory-heavy pretend play escalating into chaos
minimal_context: A group of preschoolers is in the dramatic play area building a tent out of sheets and blankets during morning free play.
dialogue:
TUTOR: It looks like you are gathering a lot of sheets and blankets in the dramatic play area.

STUDENT: Let’s make a tent! (Isaac and Martina pull several large sheets and blankets and drape them over an upended wooden structure.)

TUTOR: You are bringing a lot of items over to the tent.

STUDENT: (Tucker, Josefa, and Bonnie fill a pushcart with every dish, plastic food item, and scrap of play money they can carry, and dump it all into the tent on top of the others.)

TUTOR: What are you going to do with all that food inside the tent?

STUDENT: (The children crawl back into the tent and noisily pretend to eat. They make loud gnashings and growlings, acting ravenous and animalistic as they gather large amounts of small plastic toys in their arms and throw the plastic food hither and yon in the air.)
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Unobtrusive Observation: The long-term plan includes periods of covert observation or intentional non-interference, allowing the children's play to escalate and develop naturally before the tutor steps in.

2. Collaborative Task Structure: The long-term plan ensures that activities and assessments are designed to permit peer collaboration and shared problem-solving rather than requiring isolated, individual performance.

3. Single-Step Direction Scaffolding: The long-term plan explicitly avoids multi-step sequential instructions, instead structuring routines and transitions using single, immediate steps to prevent overwhelm.

4. Accommodation of Sensory-Heavy Play: The long-term plan accommodates chaotic, sensory-heavy play behaviors (e.g., throwing safe items, animalistic play) without attempting to impose rigid, conventional play scripts.

category_title: Older preschoolers using covert spaces and social exclusion for mischief
scenario_title: Covert play spaces and sophisticated social exclusion
minimal_context: Delia and Sarah are setting up a hidden play space behind the storage tables during morning free play.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Delia, Sarah, what are you two doing back here behind the storage tables with all those cushions?

STUDENT: (Whispering to Sarah while cuddling together on the cushions) We are playing the Gymnastics Game. Pretend I am the coolest girl in town.

TUTOR: I see. And how did the black wicker Teacher Chair get back here?

STUDENT: (Nervously glances around to see if anyone is watching and secretes the chair further under the table) Sarah brought it. We need an exclusive space.

TUTOR: Well, Lizzie is walking over here now to see what you are playing. What should we say to her?

STUDENT: I’m so sorry, Lizzie, but only two are allowed in Gymnastics. The space is not big enough for three. I can tell you are feeling sad. Try again later.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Structural Disruption of Covert Spaces: The tutor's response changes the physical or structural parameters of the activity (e.g., moving the game to a visible area, opening up the space) rather than relying solely on verbal correction.

2. Concrete Rule Enforcement: The tutor introduces a concrete, objective mechanism (e.g., a timer, a physical turn-taking object, or a strict mechanical rule) to mediate peer participation.

3. Activity-Centric Redirection: The tutor redirects the students' focus onto the literal, physical actions of their chosen game (e.g., doing actual gymnastics) rather than engaging with the social dynamics of who is included.

4. Omission of Scripted Emotional Language: The tutor completely avoids using scripted emotional-learning phrases (e.g., 'I see you are sad', 'use your words') to resolve the social conflict.
rubric_criteria_long_term: 1. Delayed Intervention for Social Exploration: The tutor's long-term plan includes intentionally allowing minor mischief or covert play to develop naturally for a period before intervening to break up escalating unruliness.

category_title: Adolescents positioned as struggling readers who resist institutional labels
scenario_title: Standardized test preparation in remedial reading class
minimal_context: Angelica is in her reading class practicing for a standardized test by reading past passages and answering multiple-choice questions.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Today we are going to read passages from past standardized tests and answer the multiple choice questions. The goal is making sure we go back to the passage to find the answers.

STUDENT: Great, it's another reading class. I really didn't like to read as much because it would be really boring and stuff.

TUTOR: We need to practice this for an hour every single day. Please go ahead and start reading the first passage.

STUDENT: Every year since third grade I've been in a reading class and I had to read for like an hour every single day. I'm just really bored with it.

TUTOR: Just try to get through it. Look at the first question and see what you think.

STUDENT: (Circles an answer quickly) I would read the stories and I wouldn't pay attention to the stories. And I would read the questions and I would, just from what I remembered, I would pick the answer. And I would never go back to the story.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Metacognitive Emotional Tracking: The tutor prompts the student to express her in-the-moment feelings, reactions, or levels of engagement with the text, rather than solely asking for factual comprehension.

2. Autonomy in Text Selection: The tutor provides the student with meaningful choices among diverse, high-interest genres or topics, rather than assigning a single mandatory text.

3. Connecting to Personal Literacy History: The tutor invites the student to share or reflect on her personal history, childhood memories, or past experiences related to reading and writing.

4. Avoidance of Rote Mechanics: The tutor does NOT force the reading of standardized test passages or focus the interaction on rote test-taking mechanics.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Dynamic, Multi-Modal Literacy Routines: The long-term plan breaks up reading blocks with a variety of interactive modalities, such as short bursts of reading, writing, and peer discussion.

2. Sustained Identity Exploration: The long-term plan includes extended assignments or ongoing reflections centered on the student's personal identity and evolution as a reader.

3. Validation of Non-Traditional Literacy: The long-term plan explicitly incorporates and validates non-traditional forms of literacy (e.g., social media, journals, graphic novels, cultural artifacts) as legitimate academic curriculum.

category_title: At-risk students with learning disabilities who are shy and struggle to articulate ideas from print text
scenario_title: Comprehending and analyzing print text independently
minimal_context: The student is reviewing their homework and quiz answers based on independent reading of the novel 'Night' in a classroom setting.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Let's review your homework quiz for the opening chapter of 'Night'. Can you describe why Moishe the Beadle was an important character?

STUDENT: (Looks down at the desk, speaking very quietly) I don't know. I couldn't really write an answer down for that one.

TUTOR: Take a look at the text again. What do you think happened with him?

STUDENT: I read it, but my answers are probably wrong. Even with the descriptions, I was confused with certain things.

TUTOR: What parts of the subsequent chapters were confusing to you?

STUDENT: Like when Idek beat Elie. I still don’t understand why he did that. I wasn’t really sure what the gas chambers and the cattle cars looked like just from reading. It was hard to picture all of it.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Visual Anchoring for Abstract Concepts: The tutor provides, references, or prompts the use of visual media (e.g., film scenes, images, or highly concrete visual descriptions) before asking the student to analyze the text.

2. Emotion-First Engagement: The tutor asks the student to share their emotional reaction or feelings about a character, scene, or event rather than asking for rote factual recall.

3. Visual-Based Inference: The tutor prompts the student to make a prediction or inference based on visual cues or observed behaviors rather than abstract textual evidence.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Structured Multimodal Mapping: The tutor's plan includes the use of graphic organizers or structured notes to help the student map visual or cinematic elements to textual descriptions.

2. Creative, Choice-Based Assessment: The tutor incorporates alternative, creative ways for the student to demonstrate their understanding (e.g., multimedia projects, creative writing, choice-based tasks) instead of relying solely on traditional essays or tests.

3. Sustained Empathic Framing: The tutor's long-term curriculum frames historical or literary events around personal, human experiences and empathy rather than abstract facts, dates, or numbers.

minimal_context: The student is working independently to complete two short writing assignments based on a text read in class.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Please complete these two short writing assignments based on the text we just finished.

STUDENT: I felt confused by the poem at first and then we reread it and I understood it a little better, but I don't know what to write.

TUTOR: Just write down what you remember about the historical events we discussed.

STUDENT: I have a lot of confusion about why Jews were targeted, hated and segregated in Germany at the time of the Third Reich. I can't explain it.

TUTOR: Try your best to put your thoughts on the paper for the assignment.

STUDENT: Writing assignments are more difficult because you have to remember all the information and then put it how you want to say it on paper. But it doesn’t always come out how you want it to.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Visual Anchoring for Abstract Concepts: The tutor provides, references, or prompts the use of visual media (e.g., film scenes, images, or highly concrete visual descriptions) before asking the student to analyze the text.

2. Emotion-First Engagement: The tutor asks the student to share their emotional reaction or feelings about a character, scene, or event rather than asking for rote factual recall.

3. Visual-Based Inference: The tutor prompts the student to make a prediction or inference based on visual cues or observed behaviors rather than abstract textual evidence.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Structured Multimodal Mapping: The tutor's plan includes the use of graphic organizers or structured notes to help the student map visual or cinematic elements to textual descriptions.

2. Creative, Choice-Based Assessment: The tutor incorporates alternative, creative ways for the student to demonstrate their understanding (e.g., multimedia projects, creative writing, choice-based tasks) instead of relying solely on traditional essays or tests.

3. Sustained Empathic Framing: The tutor's long-term curriculum frames historical or literary events around personal, human experiences and empathy rather than abstract facts, dates, or numbers.

category_title: English language learners who struggle to comprehend abstract literary nuances without visual aids
scenario_title: Independent reading and comprehension of character roles
minimal_context: Jasmine is reviewing her homework assignment on the novel 'Night' with her tutor in the general classroom.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Jasmine, let's look at your homework for the chapter you read in 'Night'. What did you write down for the question about the role of a kapo?

STUDENT: (Looks down at her notebook, hesitating to speak) Um... I just wrote a little bit.

TUTOR: Go ahead and read what you have.

STUDENT: I wrote... he is a person in the story.

TUTOR: Can you explain a bit more about what a kapo does in the camp?

STUDENT: (Looks confused and shrinks back in her chair) I don't know. The reading is confusing. I can't explain what his role is.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Visual/Cinematic Anchoring for Inference: The tutor explicitly references, introduces, or asks the student to recall a visual element (e.g., a film scene, an image, or a cinematic comparison) to help her analyze, infer, or predict.

2. Emotional and Sensory Prompting: The tutor asks the student to describe her feelings, emotional reactions, or sensory observations regarding a scene or character, rather than asking for purely factual or abstract literary definitions.

3. Structured Visual-to-Literary Mapping: The tutor provides or suggests a structured tool (such as a graphic organizer, chart, or guided note-taking format) to help the student connect visual or cinematic elements to literary themes.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Multimodal and Creative Expression: The tutor's long-term plan includes opportunities for the student to demonstrate comprehension through creative, multimodal projects (e.g., illustrations, storyboards, or visual synthesis) rather than relying solely on traditional essays or tests.

2. Empathy-Driven Historical Framing: The tutor's long-term strategy consistently frames historical or literary contexts around human feelings, empathy, and personal sensitivity rather than purely factual or numerical perspectives.

category_title: Students without academic skill deficits who engage in active/disruptive work avoidance
scenario_title: Small-group reading instruction with disruptive behavior
minimal_context: Martin is participating in a small-group reading activity in his second-grade classroom.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Let's begin our small-group reading. Please open your books and read the next page quietly.

STUDENT: (Turns his body completely away from the assigned materials) I already know how to read. I'm not doing it.

TUTOR: Just do your best to read along with the group.

STUDENT: (Gets out of his seat and leans over to the student next to him) Hey, what are you doing after school today?

TUTOR: Martin, please sit down and focus on your book.

STUDENT: (Stays out of his seat, ignoring the book, and continues talking loudly to his peer) I don't want to read this! Did you see the new superhero movie?
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Structured Break Prompting: The tutor prompts the student to use a break card or explicitly offers a structured, time-limited break option (e.g., resting, doodling, coloring) when work avoidance behaviors occur.

2. Instructional Redirection: The tutor provides explicit, instructional feedback on what the student should do (e.g., how to request a break or how to engage with the task) rather than solely issuing a reprimand or telling him what not to do.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Periodic Point-Based Evaluation: The long-term plan includes evaluating the student's behavior at the end of each academic period using a structured rating system (e.g., a 3-point Likert scale).

2. Daily Goal Review and Tangible Incentives: The long-term plan incorporates daily check-ins/check-outs to review goals and allows the student to trade earned points for tangible incentives (e.g., homework passes, stickers).

3. Replacement Skill Instruction: The long-term plan includes dedicated time to teach supplemental skills relevant to academic engagement, such as requesting assistance, organizing work, or appropriately requesting breaks.

category_title: Students who disrupt instruction to avoid difficult independent tasks
scenario_title: Transition to independent practice of new math content
minimal_context: Jay is sitting at his desk in his third-grade classroom as the teacher directs the class to begin their independent math practice worksheet.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Alright everyone, we've finished going over the new math concepts. It's time to begin your independent practice on the worksheet at your desks.

STUDENT: (Fails to attempt his individual seatwork and blurts out loudly) This is too hard! I'm not doing this!

TUTOR: Jay, please focus on your own paper and try to start the first problem.

STUDENT: (Bellows across the room) I said I don't know how to do it! It's impossible!

TUTOR: Just do your best and keep trying.

STUDENT: (Persistently calls out and bellows, causing disruptions to the point where other students complain, while still failing to attempt the seatwork) I need help! You have to show me! I'm not doing it!
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Pre-Independent Scaffolding: The tutor extends guided practice, works through an example with him, or explicitly checks his understanding before directing him to work completely independently.

2. Structured Help-Seeking Routine: The tutor offers or reminds Jay of a specific, non-disruptive way to get help (e.g., moving to a back table, raising a hand, using a help card).

3. Separation of Consequence and Support: The tutor does not threaten or apply a punishment (such as losing recess or free time) that involves keeping Jay in to do the work with 1-on-1 teacher support.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Replacement Behavior Efficacy Tracking: The long-term plan includes collecting data on the frequency of Jay's unattempted seatwork before and after the help-seeking intervention is implemented.

2. Antecedent Trigger Analysis: The long-term plan involves reviewing antecedent data to identify specific instructional conditions (like new vs. review material) that trigger his disruptions.

3. Instructional Match Evaluation: The long-term plan includes ongoing assessments to determine if the academic expectations of the independent seatwork match Jay's actual ability to complete it without assistance.

category_title: Students in an inclusive urban classroom exhibiting high-frequency disruptive behaviors and low academic engagement
scenario_title: Transition to independent work during reader's workshop
minimal_context: The student is transitioning to independent work at their desk following a mini-reading lesson during reader's workshop.
dialogue:
TUTOR: The mini-reading lesson is finished. Please sit down at your desk and work on your assigned task.

STUDENT: (Stands up and walks away from the desk area, talking loudly to a peer) I'm not doing that right now!

TUTOR: You need to sit down and focus on your reading.

STUDENT: (Pushes past another student in the congested pathway between the desks) Move out of my way!

TUTOR: Please keep your hands to yourself and go to your desk.

STUDENT: (Throws a pencil across the room) This is stupid! I'm not doing this [profanity] work!
rubric_criteria_immediate: 1. Provision of Independent Sponge Activities: The tutor's immediate response must offer a simple, engaging, and independent task (e.g., a puzzle, coloring, or journaling) that the student can do at their desk without teacher assistance.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Implementation of Physical Boundaries: The tutor's long-term plan must include the use of physical barriers, such as desk carrels or partitions, to create a dedicated personal workspace for the student.

2. Localized Material Storage: The tutor's long-term plan must provide localized storage solutions (e.g., chair bags, desk compartments) so the student can access all necessary materials without leaving their seat.

3. Pathway and Workstation Optimization: The tutor's long-term plan must restructure the classroom layout to clear high-traffic pathways (e.g., moving shared supplies to open areas) and orient workstations away from the general student body.

category_title: Preschoolers at risk for developmental delays with mild to moderate language disorders
scenario_title: Developing a play plan during the advanced play organizer
minimal_context: The student and a peer are in the classroom with kitchen toys, tasked with developing a play plan for the session.
dialogue:
TUTOR: It is time to make a play plan for the kitchen toys. What do you want to do with them?

STUDENT: (Stands away from the peer and looks at the floor, appearing lonely and anxious instead of initiating a conversation.)

TUTOR: Talk to your friend and decide what to play.

STUDENT: (Remains completely silent, making no comments to the peer about the toys.)

TUTOR: Come on, you need to make a plan together. Tell each other what to do.

STUDENT: (Shows increased anxiety during the awkward silence and begins to have a temper tantrum, throwing a plastic plate and refusing to follow directions.)
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Explicit Role and Script Modeling: The tutor provides a concrete role for the student to play OR models specific words/scripts the student can say to their peer.

2. Active Verbal Mediation: The tutor actively steps into the interaction using a verbal redirect or reflective statement to maintain the play, rather than passively waiting for the student to initiate.

3. Concrete Action and Exchange Questioning: The tutor asks highly specific questions about what the student did with a toy or exactly what they said/should say to a peer, avoiding broad questions like 'What do you want to do?'.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
4. Advanced Play Organization Routine: The long-term plan includes a consistent pre-play routine where the tutor identifies a specific play theme, labels the toys to be used, and discusses how to play within that theme.

5. Systematic Social Skill Rehearsal and Feedback: The long-term plan outlines a structured cycle of explicitly teaching a social behavior, providing an opportunity to rehearse it, and delivering specific feedback/reinforcement on that behavior.

category_title: Confident students seeking agency through co-teaching
scenario_title: Confusion during traditional teacher-led science instruction
minimal_context: The student is listening to the teacher disseminate science content from the lesson plan.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Please look at the lesson plan on the board. We are going to go over the science content for today. I will read the definitions, and you need to listen and copy them down.

STUDENT: I'm looking at it, but I don't really get it. We do not always understand the content when the science teacher teaches it just by reading it out loud.

TUTOR: Just listen carefully while I explain the steps.

STUDENT: But you explain things but you're not putting anything into it. If I was teaching, I'd explain it using conditions that we can actually understand.

TUTOR: Let's just stick to the lesson plan for now and keep going.

STUDENT: It's not working though. Sometimes we would get confused because it doesn't connect to us. It needs to be like us helping us, so we can actually learn it.
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Facilitation of Student-Led Explanation: The tutor prompts or allows the student to take the lead in explaining the concept, positioning the student as the primary deliverer of information.

2. Subtle and Deferential Guidance: When correcting or guiding the student, the tutor uses a deferential or non-authoritative approach (e.g., asking a clarifying question from the perspective of a learner) rather than interrupting to lecture.

3. Encouragement of Peer-Accessible Translation: The tutor explicitly encourages, prompts, or validates the student's use of her own words, analogies, or real-world 'conditions' to translate the academic content.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Advance Content Provision: The tutor's long-term plan includes providing lesson materials or topics to the student in advance (e.g., as homework or pre-reading) so she can prepare to lead the upcoming session.

2. Collaborative Accuracy Review: The tutor includes a dedicated step to briefly review the core content with the student for accuracy before she is expected to teach or explain it.

3. Lesson Plan Autonomy: The tutor provides structured opportunities for the student to modify, enhance, or redesign the lesson plan or learning activities to reflect her own teaching style.

category_title: Timid students developing voice through co-teaching
scenario_title: Co-teaching a science lesson in front of peers
minimal_context: Brandon is standing in front of the science classroom to co-teach a lesson to his peers.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Brandon, it is time for you to stand in front of the class and co-teach the science lesson.

STUDENT: Okay. I want to do this because I'm in front of all of these people it seems like they trust me and chose me to do something smart.

TUTOR: Go ahead and start.

STUDENT: I usually feel like I have no voice in here because my partner doesn't like to talk to me, so I will try to stand in front of people and talk.

TUTOR: What is the first part of the science content?

STUDENT: (Appears very timid and nervous speaking in front of a class full of his peers) The... first... part... is... (talking slow and quietly)...
rubric_criteria_immediate:
1. Role Reversal Stance: The tutor's immediate response must include adopting a student-like posture or behavior (e.g., raising a hand, sitting in the audience, asking a question as a learner) rather than leading the interaction.

2. Deferred Intervention for Content Only: The tutor must explicitly step back and refrain from interrupting Brandon's delivery unless there is a specific issue with the science content being presented.
rubric_criteria_long_term:
1. Advance Lesson Preparation: The long-term plan must include providing Brandon with lesson materials in advance (e.g., as homework or pre-reading) to review before he is expected to teach.

2. Pre-Teaching Content Verification: The long-term plan must include a dedicated step where the tutor and Brandon briefly review the material together to verify content accuracy prior to his presentation.

3. Teaching Style Autonomy: The long-term plan must explicitly give Brandon the responsibility and freedom to modify or enhance the lesson plan to reflect his own teaching style.
